line: Ernesto Villaseñor. In Guadalajara I was a notario for twenty-two years. Here I prepare taxes. Permit me to say it now, so nobody confuses the two.
choice2: Nice to meet you, Don Ernesto.
choice3: I don't really need a tax guy.

line: In Mexico a notario is a lawyer the state appoints. Here a notary stamps your signature for five dollars. People see 'notario' on a flyer and pay a stranger two thousand.
choice3: Good to know. I should go.

line: Precisely. Every spring someone comes to my table with a receipt and nothing filed. I cannot fix it. I can only send them to the legal aid office on Fifth.
choice2: That must be hard to see.
choice3: I'll let you get back to it.

line: Forty dollars. Twenty for students, nothing for the widows of men I knew. The parish gives me the table. I bring my own pens. They walk off otherwise.
choice1: I'll come see you in February.

line: My granddaughter plays violin in the school orchestra. Third chair. I said third is a fine chair. She has not spoken to me since Tuesday.
The library keeps the tax forms in a drawer nobody can find. I have explained to the young man at the desk where they are. Twice.
You ask good questions. Most people ask me only about their refund. Tell me honestly: do you keep your receipts?
Three clients asked me this week to take their returns out of my files. As if paper could make them invisible. I told them: filing is the proof you were here.
The new rule lets the clinic help people apply for benefits. Good. Now I will have twice the people at my table asking which line is line 11.
You are always here lately. Good. The hall needs young people who can lift tables. Also ones who can read a W-2, but I don't hope for miracles.
Pilar says you're at the library more than the hall now. It's a good library. Very complete. Except the drawer with the forms.
Don Ernesto inclines his head, very correctly, and goes back to his papers.
choice1: Don Ernesto, I owe you an apology.

line: One moment. I am adding a column. If I lose the column, I lose the morning.
